course.title: Ethical Hacking Fundamentals
course.description: A practical, authorization-first foundation in ethical hacking and penetration testing. The course teaches engagement scoping, reconnaissance, network and service enumeration, vulnerability discovery and validation, web and API security testing, controlled exploitation concepts, evidence handling, reporting, remediation, and retesting. Hands-on activities use synthetic data, local labs, intentionally vulnerable systems, and dedicated test accounts; the course does not require attacking public or third-party systems.
prerequisites: Basic networking concepts such as IP addresses, ports, HTTP, and DNS are helpful but are introduced where required.
A local lab environment is recommended for hands-on exercises; students should only test systems they own or are explicitly authorized to assess.
learningOutcomes: Define ethical hacking, vulnerability assessment, penetration testing, and rules of engagement.
Build a scoped asset inventory and perform controlled reconnaissance and network/service enumeration.
Interpret scanner results and validate vulnerabilities using evidence rather than assumptions.
Apply OWASP-based web application and API security testing concepts to authorized applications.
Design safe, minimal exploit-validation procedures using dedicated lab targets and test accounts.
Produce evidence-driven findings with severity, confidence, impact, remediation, and retest criteria.
Execute a complete local reporting workflow and explain how ethical hacking integrates with remediation and risk management.

modules.title: Foundations, Ethics, and Engagement Scope
modules.description: Establish the legal, ethical, technical, and operational boundaries of authorized security testing.

lessons.title: What Ethical Hacking Is—and Is Not
lessons.description: Define ethical hacking as authorized security testing performed to discover and communicate weaknesses so they can be reduced.
learningObjectives: Define ethical hacking, vulnerability assessment, penetration testing, and security assessment.
Explain why authorization and scope are prerequisites for testing.
Differentiate defensive validation from unauthorized intrusion.

notes.text: Ethical hacking is a testing activity performed with permission and a defined objective. The tester is accountable for respecting the agreed scope, protecting sensitive information, and minimizing disruption.

items: Vulnerability assessment emphasizes discovering and characterizing weaknesses; penetration testing adds controlled attempts to demonstrate exploitability and impact.
A test result is evidence about the tested condition, not proof that every untested path is secure.
Use lab systems or explicitly authorized targets for all hands-on work.

notes.text: Never scan or test systems simply because they are reachable. Reachability is not authorization.

quiz.question: What is the most important prerequisite before actively testing a third-party system?
options: A written authorization and defined scope
quiz.answer: A written authorization and defined scope
quiz.explanation: Authorization and scope establish what may be tested, how, and under what conditions.

summary: Ethical hacking is permission-based security testing.
Scope and safety rules are part of the technical methodology, not administrative paperwork alone.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

lessons.title: Rules of Engagement and Scope Control
lessons.description: Turn a broad testing request into explicit target, timing, communication, and safety constraints.
learningObjectives: Create in-scope and out-of-scope asset lists.
Specify test windows, rate limits, prohibited actions, and escalation contacts.
Explain stop conditions for disruptive findings.

items: Scope should identify domains, IP ranges, applications, accounts, environments, and exclusions where applicable.
Rules of engagement should state allowed techniques, test windows, emergency contacts, logging expectations, and evidence-handling requirements.
Stop conditions protect availability and client operations.

notes.text:
Example scope document fragment:

In scope: app.lab.example, 192.0.2.10/32
Out of scope: payment.example, production database
Test window: 22:00–02:00 UTC
Rate limit: 5 requests/second
Stop if: service instability, data corruption, or unexpected third-party impact

quiz.question: Why should a rules-of-engagement document include stop conditions?
options: To prevent unnecessary operational impact and define when testing must pause
quiz.answer: To prevent unnecessary operational impact and define when testing must pause
quiz.explanation: Stop conditions provide objective safety boundaries for the engagement.

summary: Scope documents convert authorization into actionable constraints.
Testing discipline includes knowing when not to continue.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

lessons.title: Threat Modeling and Attack Surface
lessons.description: Use assets, trust boundaries, entry points, and business impact to prioritize what to test first.
learningObjectives: Identify assets and trust boundaries.
Map external and internal attack surface components.
Prioritize testing based on exposure and business criticality.

notes.text: A useful threat model is not a list of generic attacks. It connects assets, actors, entry points, trust boundaries, and consequences. For testing, this produces a defensible order of operations.

items: Internet-facing services often deserve early review because they have broad exposure.
Administrative interfaces and sensitive data flows are high-value paths.
Assumptions should be written down so another tester can reproduce the prioritization.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a trust boundary in threat modeling?
options: To mark a physical office wall
To identify where data, privileges, or trust assumptions change
quiz.answer: To identify where data, privileges, or trust assumptions change
quiz.explanation: Trust boundaries highlight places where security assumptions change and deserve scrutiny.

summary: Threat modeling gives the assessment a reasoned order.
Business impact and exposure should influence testing priorities.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework

lessons.title: Evidence, Notes, and Data Handling
lessons.description: Create reproducible evidence while protecting client data and maintaining chain-of-custody awareness.
learningObjectives: Capture timestamps, commands, responses, and screenshots consistently.
Hash collected files when integrity verification matters.
Minimize retention of unnecessary sensitive data.

items: Record timezone and system time assumptions when building evidence timelines.
Use least-data principles: collect what supports the finding and avoid unnecessary secrets or personal data.
A hash can detect later changes; it does not itself establish authenticity or legal admissibility.

notes.text:
sha256sum evidence.txt
# Record: timestamp, source, collector, method, SHA-256

quiz.question: What does hashing an evidence file primarily provide?
quiz.answer: An integrity check value
quiz.explanation: A cryptographic hash can be recomputed later to detect changes.

summary: Evidence should be reproducible and minimized.
Integrity checks support trustworthy handling of collected artifacts.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

tasks.title: Write a Rules-of-Engagement Summary
tasks.description: Create a one-page ROE for a fictional web assessment.
tasks.problemStatement: Convert a business request into testable boundaries, including targets, exclusions, timing, rate limits, communication, and stop conditions.
requirements: Use only fictional domains and documentation IP ranges.
Do not include personal data or real credentials.
tasks.hint: Start with what the tester is allowed to touch, then define how testing may occur.
tasks.solutionCode: Return a markdown document with the sections Scope, Exclusions, Schedule, Allowed Methods, Prohibited Actions, Contacts, Stop Conditions, and Evidence Handling.
tasks.solutionExplanation: A complete ROE turns permission into concrete technical limits that a tester can follow consistently.

modules.title: Reconnaissance and Information Gathering
modules.description: Perform controlled discovery of externally visible information and build a target profile without crossing authorization boundaries.

lessons.title: Passive vs Active Reconnaissance
lessons.description: Differentiate collection that does not directly interact with the target from direct probing.
learningObjectives: Classify common reconnaissance activities as passive or active.
Explain why passive collection can still expose sensitive information.
Choose the least intrusive method that answers the current question.

items: Passive sources can include public documentation, DNS records, certificate transparency, and organization-published information.
Active reconnaissance sends traffic to the target and therefore consumes scope and operational risk.
Recon should produce a target inventory rather than an unstructured pile of facts.

practicals.title: Build a Passive Recon Worksheet
practicals.description: Create a passive reconnaissance record from a fictional organization profile without directly probing any live target.
steps: Use the provided fictional organization name and documentation data in the lesson scenario.
Record discovered domains, service names, technologies, and public-facing business functions.
For each observation, record source, timestamp, confidence, and whether the asset is confirmed in scope.
Identify two observations that require authorization confirmation before active testing.
practicals.solution:
Example solution structure:
asset: app.lab.example
type: hostname
source: engagement-provided inventory
confidence: high
scope_status: confirmed
next_step: controlled service enumeration
practicals.output: A normalized reconnaissance worksheet with provenance and explicit scope status.

quiz.question: Why is passive reconnaissance often preferred first?
options: It can reduce unnecessary interaction with the target while building context
quiz.answer: It can reduce unnecessary interaction with the target while building context
quiz.explanation: Passive collection can establish useful context before active testing begins.

summary: Use the least intrusive discovery technique that answers the question.
Organize reconnaissance into a usable target inventory.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

lessons.title: DNS and Certificate Intelligence
lessons.description: Use DNS and certificate information to understand exposed naming and service relationships.
learningObjectives: Explain A/AAAA, CNAME, MX, and TXT records at a practical level.
Use certificate names as clues to discover authorized service names.
Avoid treating DNS data as proof of application ownership without validation.

notes.text:
# Documentation-only examples
dig A app.lab.example
dig CNAME api.lab.example
dig TXT lab.example

items: DNS often reveals service names and infrastructure relationships.
Certificate names can expose alternate hostnames; they are clues, not automatic authorization.
Document source and observation time for time-sensitive recon data.

quiz.question: What should a tester do before actively probing a hostname found during recon?
options: Confirm it is explicitly authorized or covered by the engagement scope
quiz.answer: Confirm it is explicitly authorized or covered by the engagement scope
quiz.explanation: Discovery does not expand authorization.

summary: DNS and certificates provide reconnaissance clues.
Discovered assets must be reconciled with the engagement scope before testing.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

lessons.title: Web Application Fingerprinting and Content Mapping
lessons.description: Map the application structure and technologies using safe, authorized discovery.
learningObjectives: Identify application entry points.
Build a content and function map.
Record technology fingerprints as hypotheses rather than facts.

items: Map pages, APIs, authentication flows, administrative functions, and static assets.
Fingerprinting can use response headers, content patterns, and normal application behavior.
Do not disclose client details in public notes or repositories.

quiz.question: Why should technology fingerprints be treated as hypotheses?
options: Applications can obscure or alter identifying information
quiz.answer: Applications can obscure or alter identifying information
quiz.explanation: Fingerprints are clues that require corroboration.

summary: Build a functional map before testing individual weaknesses.
Use multiple observations to support technology hypotheses.

lessons.title: Controlled Recon Tools: Nmap and HTTP Proxies
lessons.description: Understand the role of common recon tools while keeping their use constrained to authorized targets.
learningObjectives: Describe Nmap host and service discovery capabilities.
Explain the role of an intercepting proxy in web testing.
Select scan intensity and tooling based on scope and risk.

notes.text:
# Lab-only examples against a target you own
nmap -sT -Pn 192.0.2.10
curl -I https://app.lab.example/

# Proxy-based workflow
Browser -> local intercepting proxy -> authorized application
Do not copy scan commands onto arbitrary internet hosts. Use a local VM, an explicitly authorized test host, or a dedicated training range.

quiz.question: What is an intercepting proxy mainly useful for during web testing?
options: Observing and modifying HTTP requests and responses within an authorized test
quiz.answer: Observing and modifying HTTP requests and responses within an authorized test
quiz.explanation: Interception provides visibility into application-layer traffic during testing.

summary: Nmap supports controlled discovery; proxies support web traffic inspection.
Tool capability never expands the authorized scope.

tasks.title: Build an Authorized Recon Inventory
tasks.description: Create an inventory from a small fictional target dataset.
tasks.problemStatement: Given hostnames, IPs, and service observations, normalize them into an asset list with owner, exposure, evidence source, and scope status.
requirements: Use only the scenario data provided in the task.
tasks.hint: Keep discovery separate from authorization status.
tasks.solutionCode: Provide a CSV or JSON inventory with fields asset, type, exposure, observation, evidence_source, and scope_status.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The inventory becomes the handoff artifact for later enumeration and testing.

modules.title: Network and Service Enumeration
modules.description: Enumerate authorized hosts and services carefully enough to form a reliable exposure picture.

lessons.title: Host Discovery and Port States
lessons.description: Understand what host discovery and port states mean operationally.
learningObjectives: Explain open, closed, and filtered TCP port states.
Choose host-discovery methods appropriate to the network context.
Avoid interpreting scanner results without context.

items: Open usually means an application is listening and accepted the probe.
Closed means reachable but no application is listening on that port.
Filtered means a packet filter or other control prevented a definitive determination.

practicals.title: Interpret a Controlled Nmap Result
practicals.description: Analyze a fictional Nmap result and determine which services deserve validation in an authorized lab.
steps: Review the sample result containing ports 22, 80, 443, and 8080.
Classify each port as open, closed, or filtered according to the supplied output.
Compare the services with the fictional architecture statement.
Identify one unexpected service and write the safest next validation step.
practicals.solution:
Example conclusion:
22/tcp -> SSH -> expected on management segment only
80/tcp -> HTTP -> expected for redirect/service role
443/tcp -> HTTPS -> expected public web service
8080/tcp -> HTTP-alt -> unexpected; confirm ownership and scope before deeper testing
practicals.output: A short evidence-based exposure analysis, not an exploitation attempt.

quiz.question: What does an 'open' TCP port generally indicate?
options: An application is listening and accepted the probe
quiz.answer: An application is listening and accepted the probe
quiz.explanation: Open describes transport-level reachability to a listening service; it does not imply vulnerability.

summary: Port state is an observation, not a vulnerability verdict.
Enumerate only services justified by the authorized scope.

lessons.title: Service and Version Identification
lessons.description: Identify services and versions to support vulnerability correlation and later validation.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of service/version detection.
Record banner or fingerprint evidence with timestamps.
Distinguish observed version evidence from vendor metadata or assumptions.

notes.text: Version detection can create additional traffic. Use it only where the engagement permits the technique and where the added traffic is acceptable.

quiz.question: Why is version evidence useful in vulnerability assessment?
options: It supports matching observed software to relevant advisories and configuration guidance
It removes the need for validation
quiz.answer: It supports matching observed software to relevant advisories and configuration guidance
quiz.explanation: Accurate version evidence narrows the set of relevant security information.

summary: Service identification improves vulnerability correlation.
Evidence quality matters more than a guessed version string.

lessons.title: Network Segmentation and Exposure Analysis
lessons.description: Use enumerated services to reason about boundaries and unexpected exposure.
learningObjectives: Identify services that should not be internet-facing.
Compare observed exposure with intended architecture.
Document segmentation gaps without assuming compromise.

items: An administrative service exposed outside its intended management network can be a material finding.
Unexpected exposure should be validated against architecture and ownership records.
A finding should explain business impact, not only technical awkwardness.

quiz.question: What makes an exposed management service especially important to review?
options: It can create a high-impact administrative entry point if access controls are weak
quiz.answer: It can create a high-impact administrative entry point if access controls are weak
quiz.explanation: Administrative interfaces can carry high privilege and therefore deserve careful exposure review.

summary: Exposure findings should connect technical access to business impact.
Architecture context helps distinguish intended from unintended exposure.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

lessons.title: Network Enumeration Task Design
lessons.description: Design repeatable enumeration sequences that minimize unnecessary traffic.
learningObjectives: Sequence lightweight discovery before deeper probes.
Set explicit port, host, and timing limits.
Capture commands and outputs so another tester can reproduce the result.

items: Confirm target is in scope.
Perform limited host/port discovery.
Identify candidate services.
Run deeper version detection only where needed.
Validate interesting results manually.
Record evidence and stop conditions.

quiz.question: Why should a tester start with lightweight discovery?
options: It reduces unnecessary traffic and focuses deeper testing on relevant services
quiz.answer: It reduces unnecessary traffic and focuses deeper testing on relevant services
quiz.explanation: Progressive discovery improves safety and efficiency.

summary: Use progressive disclosure: broad enough to map, narrow enough to stay safe.
Reproducibility requires recording tools, options, targets, and timestamps.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

tasks.title: Analyze a Port-Scan Result
tasks.description: Interpret a sample Nmap result and turn it into security observations.
tasks.problemStatement: Classify each discovered service as expected, questionable, or requiring validation based on a provided architecture statement.
requirements: Do not infer vulnerabilities solely from port numbers.
tasks.hint: Compare the scan to the intended architecture first.
tasks.solutionCode: Return a table with host, port, observed service, expected?, concern, and next validation step.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task builds analytical discipline: scanner output is input to reasoning, not the final finding.

modules.title: Vulnerability Discovery and Validation
modules.description: Move from scanner output to verified, risk-aware vulnerability findings.

lessons.title: What a Vulnerability Scanner Actually Does
lessons.description: Understand signatures, configuration checks, version matching, and the limits of automated discovery.
learningObjectives: Describe common scanner detection strategies.
Explain false positives and false negatives.
Identify evidence needed to validate a scanner result.

items: Scanners may use version matching, configuration tests, protocol responses, and other indicators.
A scanner can miss conditions that depend on business logic or unusual application states.
A finding should be validated before it is represented as confirmed in a report.

quiz.question: Why can automated vulnerability scans produce false positives?
options: A detection signal can match a condition that is not actually exploitable or applicable in the environment
quiz.answer: A detection signal can match a condition that is not actually exploitable or applicable in the environment
quiz.explanation: Detection logic is evidence, but contextual validation is still needed.

summary: Treat scanner results as candidate findings until verified.
Validation considers applicability, reachability, and compensating controls.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

lessons.title: CVE, CWE, and Vulnerability Identity
lessons.description: Connect vulnerability records to root causes and standardized identifiers.
learningObjectives: Differentiate CVE from CWE.
Use NVD and vendor advisories as vulnerability references.
Avoid using a generic weakness identifier as proof of a specific CVE.

items: CVE identifies a publicly disclosed vulnerability record; CWE describes classes of software weakness and root cause.
NVD enriches public CVE records with additional analysis and references.
A vulnerability report should use the most specific identifier supported by evidence.

quiz.question: Which identifier describes a class of software weakness rather than a single disclosed vulnerability?
quiz.answer: CWE
quiz.explanation: CWE classifies weakness types; CVE identifies specific disclosed vulnerability records.

summary: CVE and CWE answer different questions.
Use identifiers precisely and cite authoritative records.

resources.title: MITRE CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses

lessons.title: CVSS v4.0 and Contextual Risk
lessons.description: Use CVSS appropriately while keeping environmental risk and exploit activity in view.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of CVSS v4.0.
Distinguish standardized severity metrics from organization-specific risk.
Incorporate exposure, asset criticality, and compensating controls into prioritization.

items: CVSS is a standardized framework for communicating vulnerability severity.
Environmental context can change how an organization prioritizes a vulnerability.
Patch priority should consider more than one score, including business impact and active exploitation intelligence.

notes.text: Do not use a CVSS score as a complete substitute for organizational risk assessment.

quiz.question: What is a key limitation of using only CVSS Base severity for patch prioritization?
options: Base metrics do not fully represent the organization's asset criticality and exposure
quiz.answer: Base metrics do not fully represent the organization's asset criticality and exposure
quiz.explanation: Environmental and operational context can change the practical priority.

summary: Use CVSS for severity communication, not as the only risk input.
Prioritization should reflect the actual environment and threat context.

lessons.title: Exploitability Validation Without Causing Harm
lessons.description: Demonstrate a weakness safely using the minimum proof necessary in an authorized lab.
learningObjectives: Choose a minimal proof-of-concept objective.
Define safety checks before validation.
Stop once sufficient evidence has been obtained.

items: A good validation proves the security condition with the least intrusive action that establishes the claim.
Do not dump secrets, destroy data, establish persistence, or pivot beyond the authorized test objective.
Capture the exact precondition, test input, observed result, and remediation state.

notes.text:
Validation record:
Precondition: authenticated test account can request record 1001
Test: request record 1002 using the same session
Observed: response returned record not owned by test account
Impact: horizontal authorization boundary bypass
Stop condition: once unauthorized access is confirmed

quiz.question: When should a tester stop exploit validation?
options: Only after compromising the whole environment
Once sufficient evidence proves the finding and continued testing adds unnecessary risk
quiz.answer: Once sufficient evidence proves the finding and continued testing adds unnecessary risk
quiz.explanation: Minimal necessary proof is safer and usually sufficient for reporting.

summary: Exploit validation should be minimal, controlled, and evidence-driven.
Proof is a means to establish a finding, not a goal of maximum compromise.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

tasks.title: Validate a Scanner Finding
tasks.description: Turn a fictional scanner alert into a confirmed, rejected, or needs-more-evidence finding.
tasks.problemStatement: Given a version finding, asset criticality, configuration snapshot, and vendor advisory, determine the proper finding state and document the evidence.
requirements: Use only the supplied scenario evidence.
tasks.hint: Ask what observation would prove or disprove the finding.
tasks.solutionCode: Return a finding record with status, evidence, confidence, risk, and next step.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution demonstrates evidence-based validation and avoids overstating scanner output.

modules.title: Web Application Security Testing
modules.description: Apply the OWASP testing framework to authentication, authorization, session, input, error-handling, and business-logic review in authorized applications.

lessons.title: Web Testing Methodology and Information Gathering
lessons.description: Map web application functionality and entry points before probing security controls.
learningObjectives: Build a functional application map.
Identify authenticated and unauthenticated attack surfaces.
Create a test hypothesis from observed workflows.

items: OWASP WSTG organizes testing into information gathering, configuration, identity, authentication, authorization, session management, input validation, error handling, cryptography, business logic, and client-side areas.
Start with the application workflow so security tests map to actual behavior.

quiz.question: Why map application entry points before testing?
options: To understand where input, authentication, authorization, and business logic can be exercised
quiz.answer: To understand where input, authentication, authorization, and business logic can be exercised
quiz.explanation: Entry-point mapping gives structure to test coverage.

summary: OWASP WSTG provides a structured web testing framework.
Functional understanding precedes targeted security testing.

lessons.title: Authentication and Session Management Testing
lessons.description: Evaluate login, logout, session issuance, timeout, recovery, and credential-handling controls.
learningObjectives: Test authentication flows against stated requirements.
Review session identifiers, invalidation, timeout, and cookie attributes.
Recognize account-enumeration and recovery risks.

items: Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides what that identity may access.
Session security includes issuance, storage, rotation, expiration, invalidation, and protection in transit.
Password reset and account recovery flows deserve security review because they can bypass the primary login path.

quiz.question: Which property should a secure logout operation achieve?
options: Invalidate the server-side session or otherwise prevent continued use of the session
quiz.answer: Invalidate the server-side session or otherwise prevent continued use of the session
quiz.explanation: Logout should end the active session according to the application's session model.

summary: Authentication and session management are connected but distinct test areas.
Recovery flows deserve the same scrutiny as login flows.

lessons.title: Authorization and Access-Control Testing
lessons.description: Test whether users can access only the objects and actions they are permitted to use.
learningObjectives: Differentiate authentication failures from authorization failures.
Test horizontal and vertical access boundaries safely.
Document the exact resource and permission boundary violated.

notes.text:
Safe authorization test pattern:
1. Log in as test-user-A.
2. Access a record owned by A.
3. Request a record owned by test-user-B using the same session.
4. Stop after the server either correctly denies or incorrectly reveals the object.
5. Do not modify or delete data.
Use dedicated test accounts and test records. Never use another real user's data as a test fixture.

practicals.title: Test Object-Level Authorization in a Lab
practicals.description: Use two synthetic test accounts and two synthetic records to validate server-side object authorization without modifying data.
steps: Create or use test-user-A and test-user-B in a dedicated lab application.
Access record-A as user A and confirm normal authorized behavior.
Using the same user-A session, request synthetic record-B.
Record the HTTP status and response behavior.
Stop immediately after the application either correctly denies access or demonstrates an authorization failure.
practicals.solution:
Expected secure behavior:
user A -> record A: allowed
user A -> record B: denied (for example, 403 or an application-specific safe response)
No record is modified or deleted.
practicals.output: Evidence showing whether the authorization boundary is correctly enforced.

quiz.question: A logged-in test user can read another test user's record by changing an ID. What does this most directly demonstrate?
quiz.answer: Broken object-level authorization
quiz.explanation: The application failed to enforce authorization for the requested object.

summary: Authorization must be enforced at the resource/action boundary.
Dedicated test accounts make access-control testing safer and clearer.

lessons.title: Input Validation, Injection, and Error Handling
lessons.description: Test whether untrusted input is validated and safely handled across application contexts.
learningObjectives: Identify input locations and expected data types.
Explain injection risks at a conceptual level.
Use benign test values to confirm validation behavior and error handling.

items: Validation checks whether input meets expected requirements; parameterized queries and context-aware encoding address separate downstream risks.
Errors should not disclose secrets, stack traces, or internal connection details.
Testing should begin with benign boundary values before any higher-risk proof is considered.

notes.text:
Boundary cases:
empty
maximum-length expected input
unexpected character class
invalid numeric value
missing required field

quiz.question: What is a good initial strategy for testing an input field?
options: Start with benign boundary and type-confusion cases that test validation behavior
quiz.answer: Start with benign boundary and type-confusion cases that test validation behavior
quiz.explanation: Low-impact cases reveal validation behavior before any higher-risk testing.

summary: Input testing starts with expected types, boundaries, and benign invalid cases.
Error messages are also security-relevant outputs.

lessons.title: Business Logic and Client-Side Testing
lessons.description: Find security failures that scanners often miss because they depend on workflow or browser behavior.
learningObjectives: Model business invariants and sequence-dependent rules.
Test duplicate, reordered, or missing workflow steps safely.
Review client-side controls without treating them as authoritative security boundaries.

items: Business-logic flaws often involve valid inputs used in an invalid sequence or context.
Client-side checks improve user experience but security decisions must be enforced server-side.
Use non-destructive test accounts and transactions when probing workflow invariants.

quiz.question: Why can business-logic vulnerabilities be missed by generic scanners?
options: They depend on application-specific workflows and invariants
quiz.answer: They depend on application-specific workflows and invariants
quiz.explanation: Generic tools cannot fully infer every intended workflow rule.

summary: Security testing must include application-specific reasoning.
Client controls should never be the sole enforcement point.

tasks.title: Create a Web Application Test Matrix
tasks.description: Create a test matrix based on the application functions and security boundaries.
tasks.problemStatement: Map each application function to relevant WSTG categories, test accounts, expected controls, evidence, and status.
tasks.hint: Build the matrix from business functions, not tool names.
tasks.solutionCode: Return a matrix with Function, User Role, WSTG Area, Test Case, Expected Result, Evidence, and Status.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The matrix makes coverage measurable and helps avoid blind spots.

modules.title: API, Authentication, and Modern Application Surfaces
modules.description: Assess API-specific authorization, rate limits, schema validation, and sensitive business flows using OWASP guidance.

lessons.title: API Discovery and Schema Understanding
lessons.description: Map REST-style endpoints, methods, parameters, schemas, and trust boundaries.
learningObjectives: Identify API endpoints and HTTP methods.
Review request/response schemas and authentication requirements.
Build an API inventory that distinguishes documented from observed endpoints.

items: APIs often expose direct object identifiers and machine-readable schemas, making authorization testing especially important.
Documented endpoints are not necessarily the complete attack surface.
Inventory should include method, path, authentication state, object identifiers, and expected role.

quiz.question: Which API property should be recorded alongside an endpoint path?
options: Only the color of the UI
HTTP method, authentication state, and authorization expectation
quiz.answer: HTTP method, authentication state, and authorization expectation
quiz.explanation: These details define the security context of an endpoint.

summary: API inventory requires more than URLs.
Authorization expectations should be explicit for each sensitive endpoint.

lessons.title: Object-Level and Function-Level Authorization
lessons.description: Apply API authorization testing to both data objects and privileged functions.
learningObjectives: Test object-level authorization boundaries.
Test function-level authorization for privileged operations.
Use role-based test accounts and synthetic objects.

items: Object-level authorization asks whether the caller may access a particular object.
Function-level authorization asks whether the caller may invoke an operation at all.
Testing both levels catches cases where an application protects the API broadly but not each object or action.

quiz.question: What is function-level authorization concerned with?
options: Whether a user can invoke an action such as admin-only account management
Whether DNS can resolve a name
quiz.answer: Whether a user can invoke an action such as admin-only account management
quiz.explanation: Function-level authorization controls which operations a principal may perform.

summary: API authorization exists at multiple decision points.
Use least privilege and dedicated test roles to validate boundaries.

lessons.title: Rate Limiting and Sensitive Business Flows
lessons.description: Assess abuse resistance without generating harmful traffic.
learningObjectives: Explain why rate limits protect availability and sensitive workflows.
Design low-volume rate-limit tests in a lab or authorized environment.
Differentiate abuse prevention from authorization.

items: Rate limiting can reduce automated abuse of resource-intensive or sensitive operations.
Business-flow protections may also require quotas, device or account signals, transaction limits, or workflow controls.
A test should measure policy behavior with small, safe request volumes rather than attempting service degradation.

notes.text:
Low-volume test concept:
10 requests over a controlled interval
Observe status codes, headers, and application behavior
Stop if latency or errors increase materially

quiz.question: What is a key difference between authorization and rate limiting?
options: Authorization decides whether an action is permitted; rate limiting constrains request frequency or volume
quiz.answer: Authorization decides whether an action is permitted; rate limiting constrains request frequency or volume
quiz.explanation: They solve different security problems and are complementary controls.

summary: Rate limiting is an abuse-resistance control, not an authorization mechanism.
Keep volume low enough to protect service availability.

lessons.title: SSRF and Server-Side Fetching Controls
lessons.description: Understand the security boundary around server-side network requests without using real third-party infrastructure.
learningObjectives: Explain the SSRF threat model.
Identify server-side URL fetch features that require scrutiny.
Describe safe validation and allowlist strategies conceptually.

items: SSRF occurs when a server makes requests to a location influenced by an untrusted user in ways that cross intended trust boundaries.
Controls can include strict allowlists, network egress restrictions, canonicalization, and avoiding unnecessary fetch features.
Use a local mock endpoint for lab demonstrations instead of real internal services.

notes.text: Do not probe cloud metadata services or private network addresses unless they are explicitly part of a dedicated training lab.

quiz.question: What is the core security concern in SSRF?
options: The server can be induced to make requests across trust boundaries it should not reach
The DNS resolver is too fast
quiz.answer: The server can be induced to make requests across trust boundaries it should not reach
quiz.explanation: SSRF turns a server-side request primitive into a boundary-crossing capability.

summary: SSRF is fundamentally a trust-boundary problem.
Use safe mock services when teaching or validating the concept.

tasks.title: Assess an API Authorization Design
tasks.description: Review a fictional API policy and identify missing authorization checks.
tasks.problemStatement: The API supports records, exports, and administrative functions. Build a test plan that covers object-level and function-level authorization.
objectives: Define safe test cases and expected results.
requirements: Use synthetic object IDs and test roles only.
tasks.hint: For each endpoint ask: who, what action, which object, under what context?
tasks.solutionCode: Return an API test matrix and a short prioritized list of likely authorization gaps.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task reinforces systematic API authorization analysis without requiring exploit execution.

modules.title: Configuration, Exploitation Concepts, and Post-Validation
modules.description: Understand controlled exploitation, misconfiguration review, and the difference between proving a flaw and causing unnecessary impact.

lessons.title: Security Misconfiguration Testing
lessons.description: Review configurations that expose unnecessary functionality, credentials, debug features, or weak defaults.
learningObjectives: Identify insecure configuration patterns.
Compare observed settings with intended baselines.
Document remediation-oriented evidence.

items: Examples include unnecessary services, debug modes, default accounts, verbose errors, insecure headers, weak TLS settings, and permissive cloud or file permissions.
A configuration finding should identify the expected secure state and the observed deviation.

quiz.question: What makes a configuration finding useful?
options: Observed state, expected state, evidence, impact, and remediation
A CVSS score with no evidence
quiz.answer: Observed state, expected state, evidence, impact, and remediation
quiz.explanation: Actionable findings compare observed and expected control states.

summary: Configuration testing compares implementation against an intended secure state.
Evidence should directly support the claimed weakness.

lessons.title: Controlled Exploitation and Cleanup
lessons.description: Understand exploitation as a bounded demonstration with explicit safety controls and cleanup.
learningObjectives: Define a proof objective before exploitation.
Use test accounts and reversible actions.
Document cleanup and residual state.

items: Controlled exploitation should answer a specific question: can the weakness be demonstrated, and what minimum evidence is needed?
Prefer reversible operations and synthetic data.
Cleanup includes removing temporary files, accounts, tokens, or configuration changes created during testing.

notes.text: Do not build persistence, deploy malware, dump real credentials, or pivot to unrelated systems as part of a fundamentals course lab.

quiz.question: Why is cleanup part of exploitation safety?
options: It removes tester-created state that could affect the client environment after testing
quiz.answer: It removes tester-created state that could affect the client environment after testing
quiz.explanation: Cleanup reduces residual impact from the test itself.

summary: Exploitation should be controlled, reversible, and cleaned up.
The test objective determines when enough evidence has been obtained.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

lessons.title: Safe Metasploit and Lab Framework Use
lessons.description: Understand framework roles in a dedicated lab without extending the exercise into real-world compromise.
learningObjectives: Explain what an exploitation framework provides conceptually.
Use a deliberately vulnerable local VM or training target for framework practice.
Record module options and evidence without targeting third parties.

notes.text: Frameworks can automate payload generation, session handling, and exploitation steps. For an ethical-hacking fundamentals course, the important skill is controlled validation: understand prerequisites, choose the smallest useful demonstration, and document the result.

Lab workflow:
1. Start isolated vulnerable VM.
2. Confirm its lab-only network address.
3. Verify the exercise is in scope.
4. Run the course-approved demonstration module.
5. Capture evidence.
6. Reset the VM snapshot.
Use intentionally vulnerable machines such as a local training VM. Do not point exploitation frameworks at public hosts or production systems.

quiz.question: What is the safest environment for learning exploitation frameworks?
options: A deliberately vulnerable isolated lab you are authorized to control
A public cloud account with unknown targets
quiz.answer: A deliberately vulnerable isolated lab you are authorized to control
quiz.explanation: An isolated authorized lab provides controlled conditions and limits unintended harm.

summary: Frameworks are tools for controlled validation, not permission to attack.
Isolation and snapshots are important safety controls.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

lessons.title: Credential Testing and Password Policy Review
lessons.description: Assess authentication strength with bounded test credentials and without credential theft.
learningObjectives: Explain password policy and credential-stuffing concepts.
Design a safe test-credential set.
Recognize when testing should stop because of lockout or service-impact risk.

items: Use dedicated test credentials supplied for the assessment rather than collected user passwords.
Test password policy requirements and lockout behavior at low volume.
Never attempt to recover or reuse real users' passwords in a fundamentals exercise.

quiz.question: What should be used for safe credential testing?
options: Dedicated test accounts and approved test credentials
quiz.answer: Dedicated test accounts and approved test credentials
quiz.explanation: Dedicated test identities reduce risk and keep the exercise controlled.

summary: Credential testing should be performed with dedicated identities and explicit limits.
Account lockouts and availability are safety concerns.

tasks.title: Design a Safe Exploitation Plan
tasks.description: Create a bounded exploitation plan for one lab vulnerability.
tasks.problemStatement: Define objective, preconditions, approved technique, evidence, stop conditions, cleanup, and reset steps.
tasks.hint: If the finding is already proven, do not escalate the test simply to gain a more dramatic result.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The plan demonstrates that exploitation is a controlled validation step with safety gates.

modules.title: Reporting, Remediation, and Retesting
modules.description: Turn technical observations into decision-ready findings and verify remediation objectively.

lessons.title: Writing a High-Quality Finding
lessons.description: Structure a finding so technical teams and decision-makers can act on it.
learningObjectives: Write concise titles and evidence-based descriptions.
Explain impact in business and technical terms.
Separate evidence, inference, and recommendation.

items: A strong finding includes: title, affected asset, severity, description, evidence, impact, reproduction summary, remediation, references, and status.
Avoid overstating impact beyond the evidence.
Recommendations should be specific enough to guide remediation but not prescribe one vendor product without need.

quiz.question: Which part of a finding should explain why the issue matters to the organization?
quiz.answer: Impact
quiz.explanation: Impact connects the technical weakness to consequences.

summary: Good reports are evidence-led and action-oriented.
Separate what was observed from what is inferred.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

lessons.title: Severity, Confidence, and Risk Communication
lessons.description: Communicate finding severity without confusing confidence with impact.
learningObjectives: Differentiate severity, confidence, likelihood, and business impact.
Use standardized severity where appropriate.
Explain uncertainty clearly.

items: Severity describes the consequence and technical seriousness of a condition; confidence describes how strongly the evidence supports the finding.
A medium-severity finding with high confidence can be more actionable than a critical-sounding claim with weak evidence.
Use CVSS when appropriate and supplement it with business context.

quiz.question: What does confidence primarily communicate?
options: How certain the evidence supports the finding
quiz.answer: How certain the evidence supports the finding
quiz.explanation: Confidence expresses evidentiary certainty, not impact magnitude.

summary: Severity and confidence answer different questions.
Risk communication should preserve uncertainty instead of hiding it.

lessons.title: Remediation and Compensating Controls
lessons.description: Translate vulnerabilities into practical corrective actions and temporary risk reductions.
learningObjectives: Recommend remediation aligned to root cause.
Identify compensating controls when immediate fixes are unavailable.
Specify verification criteria for remediation.

items: Root-cause remediation is preferable to a brittle workaround.
Compensating controls reduce risk while the primary fix is pending.
Every recommendation should have a verification method, such as a configuration check or repeat test.

quiz.question: What is a compensating control?
options: A control that temporarily or alternatively reduces the same risk when the preferred fix is not yet available
quiz.answer: A control that temporarily or alternatively reduces the same risk when the preferred fix is not yet available
quiz.explanation: Compensating controls reduce residual exposure while the direct fix is pending.

summary: Remediation should address root cause where practical.
Verification criteria make retesting objective.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

lessons.title: Retesting and Closure
lessons.description: Perform focused retests to confirm that reported vulnerabilities are actually fixed.
learningObjectives: Design a retest from the original evidence and acceptance criteria.
Distinguish fixed, partially fixed, and not fixed states.
Close findings with traceable evidence.

items: Reference the original finding and affected component.
Repeat the minimal validation that established the issue.
Verify the security property or configuration state.
Capture fresh evidence.
Record the closure state and any residual risk.

quiz.question: What is the best basis for a remediation retest?
options: The original finding's evidence and acceptance criteria
quiz.answer: The original finding's evidence and acceptance criteria
quiz.explanation: Retesting should directly verify whether the original condition was removed.

summary: Retesting is a verification activity, not a second full engagement by default.
Closure requires fresh evidence and explicit status.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

tasks.title: Produce a Mini Penetration-Test Report
tasks.description: Create a short professional report from three fictional findings.
tasks.problemStatement: Write executive summary, methodology, findings, risk table, remediation priorities, and retest criteria.
tasks.hint: Readers need enough evidence to reproduce the conclusion and enough business context to prioritize the fix.
tasks.solutionCode: Submit a markdown report with an executive summary and three detailed findings.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The report demonstrates the communication skill required to turn testing into useful remediation decisions.

lessons.title: Capstone Architecture and Acceptance Criteria
lessons.description: Define the final assessment workflow and local data model before implementation.
learningObjectives: Translate an engagement scope into structured data.
Define finding fields and validation rules.
Specify acceptance criteria for report generation.

notes.text: The capstone is intentionally local-only. It processes fictional scope and finding records, validates required fields, sorts findings by severity, and generates a markdown report. This demonstrates the reporting and evidence discipline of an ethical-hacking engagement without performing offensive activity.

quiz.question: Why does the capstone validate scope data before generating the report?
options: To ensure the report reflects an explicit engagement boundary and required metadata
quiz.answer: To ensure the report reflects an explicit engagement boundary and required metadata
quiz.explanation: Scope integrity is foundational to trustworthy security-testing output.

summary: Structure first, then generate output.
The capstone models safe assessment operations rather than live exploitation.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment

lessons.title: Implementing and Testing the Reporting Workflow
lessons.description: Build, run, and validate the local report generator and its tests.
learningObjectives: Run syntax and unit tests.
Generate a report from synthetic records.
Verify findings remain traceable from source data to output.

python -m py_compile report.py
python -m pytest -q
python report.py scope.json findings.json --output report.md
Only use the included synthetic assessment data. The capstone does not require network access or live target interaction.

quiz.question: What does an automated test in the capstone primarily protect against?
options: Regressions in report generation and input validation
quiz.answer: Regressions in report generation and input validation
quiz.explanation: Automated tests verify that the local reporting logic continues to behave as specified.

summary: Testing makes the final reporting workflow reproducible.
The tool remains useful even without network access.

project.name: Authorized Web Assessment Reporting Toolkit
project.description: Create a local, evidence-driven reporting toolkit for a fictional web security assessment. The tool validates engagement scope and finding records, sorts findings by severity, and generates a structured markdown report. The final artifact demonstrates ethical engagement discipline, application-security findings, severity and confidence communication, remediation guidance, and retesting criteria without performing live scanning or exploitation.
steps: Review the synthetic scope.json and confirm that targets and exclusions are explicit.
Review findings.json and verify that each finding contains evidence, impact, remediation, and retest criteria.
Run report.py with the supplied local data and generate report.md.
Run the automated tests and syntax checks.
Add one additional synthetic finding and extend the tests to validate its required fields and ordering.
Review the generated report for overstated claims, missing evidence, and unclear remediation.
Document the final assessment workflow and identify two process improvements for a future engagement.

code.README.md:
# Authorized Web Assessment Capstone

This capstone packages a scope file, finding records, and a small report generator for a fictional web application security assessment.

Safety boundary: the project performs no network scanning, exploitation, password attacks, or external requests. It processes local assessment records only.
code.scope.json:
{
  "engagement": "WEB-LAB-001",
  "targets": ["app.lab.example"],
  "excluded_targets": ["payments.lab.example"],
  "test_window": "22:00-02:00 UTC",
  "notes": "Fictional training engagement; all data is synthetic."
}
code.findings.json:
[
  {
    "id": "F-001",
    "title": "Broken object-level authorization on test records",
    "severity": "high",
    "confidence": "high",
    "asset": "app.lab.example/api/records/{id}",
    "status": "open",
    "evidence": "Dedicated test-user-A retrieved the synthetic record owned by test-user-B when changing the record identifier.",
    "impact": "A caller may access another tenant's records if equivalent controls are absent elsewhere.",
    "remediation": "Enforce server-side object-level authorization for every record access.",
    "retest": "Repeat the cross-record access test with two isolated test identities and confirm access is denied."
  },
  {
    "id": "F-002",
    "title": "Verbose error response reveals implementation detail",
    "severity": "low",
    "confidence": "high",
    "asset": "app.lab.example/api/search",
    "status": "open",
    "evidence": "A malformed search value returned a stack-trace fragment in the test environment.",
    "impact": "Internal implementation details may aid reconnaissance.",
    "remediation": "Return a generic client-facing error and log detailed diagnostics server-side.",
    "retest": "Send the original benign malformed input and confirm the response no longer contains stack-trace details."
  }
]
code.test_report.py:
import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent

def test_report_generation():
    out = ROOT / "test-report.md"
    result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(ROOT/"report.py"), str(ROOT/"scope.json"), str(ROOT/"findings.json"), "--output", str(out)], capture_output=True, text=True)
    assert result.returncode == 0, result.stderr
    text = out.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    assert "F-001" in text
    assert "F-002" in text
    assert text.index("F-001") < text.index("F-002")
    out.unlink()

project.explanation: The project models a defensible security-assessment workflow as structured data plus deterministic validation and reporting. scope.json prevents the report from losing engagement boundaries; findings.json keeps each claim tied to evidence and remediation; report.py validates the inputs and renders a consistent markdown report; test_report.py provides regression coverage. The project intentionally avoids network access, scanning, credential attacks, exploitation, persistence, and data modification, because those actions are not necessary to demonstrate the core fundamentals of professional ethical-hacking reporting.
